title: Cerebras Stock Plunges 20% After First Earnings Report Despite Revenue Nearly Doubling
excerpt: The AI chipmaker's debut earnings beat revenue expectations but a margin guidance cut to 38-41% for 2026 spooked investors, wiping out billions in market value.
body:
• Cerebras shares fell nearly 20% after the company guided full-year 2026 gross margins to 38-41%, down from 47% in Q1, well below rivals Nvidia and AMD.
  • First-quarter revenue hit $193 million, up 94% year-over-year, and net losses narrowed from $23.9 million to $14 million.
  • CEO Andrew Feldman said the margin dip stems from temporarily renting its own systems back from a customer to add capacity faster, and that investors misread the guidance.
  • Cerebras raised $5.5 billion in May in the largest semiconductor IPO ever and has a $20 billion multi-year chip deal with OpenAI.

Cerebras Systems, the AI chipmaker that went public in May in the largest semiconductor IPO in history, saw its stock crater nearly 20% on June 25 after its debut earnings report spooked investors with lower-than-expected profit margin guidance — even as revenue nearly doubled.

The Numbers Behind the Sell-Off

First-quarter revenue came in at $193.4 million, up 94% from $99.5 million in the year-ago period and ahead of Wall Street estimates. The adjusted net loss narrowed sharply to $2.5 million, crushing analyst forecasts of a $36.75 million loss. By those measures, Cerebras delivered a clean beat.

But the forward-looking guidance told a different story. Cerebras projected full-year 2026 adjusted gross margins of 38% to 41%, a steep decline from the 47% it reported in Q1. For the second quarter specifically, it guided margins to just 36% to 38%.

Those numbers, while above analyst estimates of roughly 29.6%, pale next to the industry leaders Cerebras is trying to challenge. Nvidia runs gross margins in the mid-70% range. AMD operates in the mid-50s. Even at the top of its guidance band, Cerebras would trail both by a wide margin.

"There was a misunderstanding in the market about what our margin guidance means."

— Andrew Feldman, CEO, Cerebras Systems

Why Margins Are Shrinking

CEO Andrew Feldman pushed back on the sell-off, telling CNBC that investors had misread the company's margin trajectory. The core issue, he explained, is a deliberate capacity trade-off: Cerebras opted to temporarily rent some of its own systems back from an existing customer to bring compute capacity online faster while it builds out its own data centers.

That rental arrangement eats into margins in the near term but accelerates revenue growth. Feldman described data center capacity as being "at a premium" across the industry, calling the current environment a "dog fight" for space.

The company said it has added data centers across the United States and Canada, in France and the Nordics, and is in early talks for facilities in Israel, the UAE, Australia, Singapore, India, and Indonesia.

The OpenAI Anchor

Much of Cerebras' growth narrative hinges on its $20 billion multi-year agreement with OpenAI, under which the ChatGPT creator will deploy 750 megawatts of Cerebras chips. Feldman confirmed during the earnings call that OpenAI's GPT 5.4 is already running on Cerebras hardware. OpenAI also holds a warrant to purchase up to 33.4 million shares of Cerebras common stock.

Cerebras has also struck a deal with AWS to deploy its wafer-scale chips in Amazon's data centers, broadening its customer base beyond a single anchor client.

A Rough Start for a Record IPO

Cerebras priced its IPO at $185 per share in May, raising $5.5 billion in what it called the largest semiconductor IPO of all time. Shares briefly soared to $385 in the days following the listing. But the post-earnings drop pushed the stock to around $195.75 — just above its IPO price and roughly 49% below its post-listing peak.

Analyst reactions were mixed. Wedbush raised its price target on Cerebras to $280, citing near-zero demand risk. Morgan Stanley analyst Joseph Moore said execution on capacity deployment will be "the key driver of revenue and gross-margin upside." Both flagged that the company's wafer-scale chip architecture sidesteps some of the industry's tightest supply bottlenecks, including high-bandwidth memory and advanced chip packaging.

Ben Bajarin, CEO of Creative Strategies, offered a more cautious take, noting that Cerebras' approach of manufacturing some of the world's largest chips inherently pressures margins because such chips are difficult and expensive to produce.

What to Watch

Cerebras guided Q2 revenue to $194 million, above the $174.3 million consensus. The company's ability to bring its own data center capacity online over the next several quarters will determine whether margins recover toward Q1 levels or remain compressed.

For investors, the fundamental question is whether Cerebras' wafer-scale technology can establish a durable competitive advantage in AI inference — or whether its margin profile will keep it permanently behind the companies it is trying to unseat.
nri_angle: Cerebras is expanding data center capacity globally, including early discussions for facilities in India, as part of its push to scale AI chip deployment.
